children: U.K. economic growth jumped again in July following a strong start to the year, with activity continuing to perform strongly despite a rise in energy prices due to the war in the Middle East.

Gross domestic product rose 0.4% at the start of the third quarter, following a rise of 0.3% in June, the U.K.'s statistics agency said Friday. This beat a consensus of economists polled by The Wall Street Journal, who expected flat growth.

The data signals continued strength in the U.K. economy following a solid performance in the first half of 2026. GDP has continued to outrun expectations despite persistently elevated energy costs following the outbreak of war in the Middle East, with annualized growth of 1.7% over the second quarter outpacing the U.S.

Activity in July was driven by the services sector, while production and construction also picked up, the Office for National Statistics said. Computer programming made the largest contribution, potentially signaling a greater impact from artificial-intelligence activity on the U.K. economy.
"Many of the businesses reporting the largest turnover in July 2026 are involved in activities related to artificial intelligence and cloud computing," the agency said.
It added that hotter weather benefited some businesses while creating challenges for others.

"The U.K. growth story is becoming harder to ignore," said Sanjay Raja, an economist at Deutsche Bank, noting that annualized growth is now tracking at 2.4%. While the labor market remains weak, solid growth suggests productivity is starting to improve meaningfully, Raja added.

The result will make positive reading for new Prime Minister Andy Burnham as his government seeks to revive an economy that has struggled with low productivity and weak growth for much of the past decade.

In his first speech as U.K. treasury chief on Monday, John Healey said the economy was "turning a corner" as he outlined plans to boost growth via a program of fiscal devolution and an increased focus on business investment. Healey refused to rule out tax rises ahead of the autumn budget.
However, July's performance is likely to be a high-water mark for growth in the third quarter, said Suren Thiru, an economist at The Institute of Chartered Accountants in England and Wales.
"Higher energy bills and pre-Budget tax uncertainty expected to weigh on household spending and economic activity through August and September," he said.
Indeed, the outlook for the rest of the year will depend largely on the intensity and duration of the energy shock, and the extent to which higher inflation affects spending and investment.

Consumer-price inflation jumped in July as an escalation of conflict in Iran drove up energy prices, and is expected to rise further in the coming months, potentially putting additional pressure on household and business confidence.

Investors expect the central bank to leave its key interest rate at 3.75% when it meets later this month, but anticipate at least one hike before the end of this year. Alongside the recent jump in U.K. borrowing costs, tighter fiscal policy could weigh further on economic growth.

Still, continued momentum in July is likely to improve the outlook for 2026. Deutsche Bank expects growth of 0.4% in the third quarter, up from previous expectations of 0.1%, while annual GDP expectations are expected to rise significantly.

"Signs of further momentum coming from higher productivity and delivery of AI investment, we think can keep GDP rising further and faster in the coming years," economists at the bank said in a recent note.
